extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and general readers of American government/history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and understanding historical descriptions and procedural norms about the Continental Congress, the Articles of Confederation, and the formation of state constitutions during the American Revolution. The page is a textbook excerpt summarizing events, institutional arrangements, and problems leading to the Federal Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructions to colonial delegates (first Continental Congress)
rubrics_metrics.description: The instructions given to each colony's delegation did not speak of union or independence; they authorized delegates to consult upon the state of the colonies and to deliberate and determine upon wise and proper measures to be recommended for the recovery and establishment of their just rights and liberties and the restoration of harmony between Great Britain and the colonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These instructions tended toward reconciliation and legal measures (e.g., South Carolina authorized only 'legal' measures), though some (e.g., North Carolina) authorized delegates to 'take such measures as they may deem prudent to effect the purpose of describing American rights with certainty and guarding them from any future violation.' The limitations on delegates had moral rather than legal force because their appointing bodies were not sovereign states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and duties of local enforcement committees (non-importation boycott)
rubrics_metrics.description: A committee should be chosen in every county, city, and town 'by those who are qualified to vote for representatives in the legislature,' whose business it shall be attentively to observe the conduct of all persons touching this association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These local committees were instructed to publish the names of all citizens who violated the terms of the boycott so that violators might be publicly known and 'universally contemned.' They thereby provided a clear-cut test of allegiance and authorized tribunals to deal with refractory citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of delegates to the second Continental Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegates to the second Congress were selected by the revolutionary bodies in the colonies organized in the form of the old assemblies, conventions, or committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This delegation process produced representatives more determined in tone; instructions for the second Congress were less conciliatory and more focused on firm establishment of American rights and privileges, with some colonies granting 'full and ample power' to obtain redress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation rule under Articles of Confederation (one state, one vote)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining questions under the confederation each colony/state should have one vote regardless of area, population, and wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule reflected the Congress's decision that each state retained 'its sovereignty, freedom, and independence, and every power, jurisdiction, and right' not expressly granted to the United States in Congress assembled. The proposal for proportional voting (by numbers) was argued against by a majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural provisions of the government under the Articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Management of general interests vested in a Congress composed of not less than two nor more than seven delegates from each state, appointed as state legislatures directed, serving subject to recall, meeting annually; each state given one vote; no president or permanent executive; Congress authorized to appoint committees and act as a court of appeal in disputes between states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No confederate court was erected; Congress had limited taxing and commercial powers and states bore expense of maintaining delegates. These structural limits contributed to weaknesses and made a constitutional revision likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional recommendation for forming state governments (May 1776)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress recommended 'to the respective assemblies and conventions of the United Colonies, where no government sufficient to the exigencies of their affairs has been hitherto established, to adopt such government as shall in the opinion of the representatives of the people best conduce to the happiness and safety of their constituents in particular and America in general.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recommendation encouraged colonies to draft constitutions suited to their needs; several states thereafter drafted new instruments and some explicitly declared the dominion of Great Britain at an end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffrage and eligibility restrictions for electing constitutional convention delegates
rubrics_metrics.description: In some states/contexts electors were explicitly limited: Pennsylvania's preliminary conference excluded non-county/provincial taxpayers, those who would not take an oath to support the Revolutionary cause, and those declared enemies to the liberties of America; Maryland required freemen to be above twenty-one and meet property or trade/housekeeper qualifications (e.g., freeholders of not less than fifty acres or visible property of £40 sterling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These restrictions meant constitutional drafting was often accomplished by a limited, property-qualified minority and many provisional constitutions were not submitted to popular ratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure and ratification practices for state constitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods were irregular: only Delaware and Massachusetts had constitutions framed by specially summoned conventions confined to that function; other constitutions were drafted by bodies simultaneously maintaining order and meeting wartime exigencies, and many were not submitted for popular ratification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Pennsylvania's convention composed of county delegates excluded many voters and did not submit the constitution to popular ratification; South Carolina's 1776 instrument was temporary and later replaced in 1778; Massachusetts adopted a constitution in 1780 after deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial defects of the Articles: inability to pay public debt
rubrics_metrics.description: The Confederation's most obvious defect was its inability to pay even interest on the public debt; the confederate Congress had no immediate taxing power and depended on state legislatures to supply levies in proportion to land value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrears on domestic and foreign debt grew dramatically (e.g., 1784-89 domestic arrears rose from $3,109,000 to $11,493,858). Congress could only recommend contributions and often had to beg states, receiving far less than requisitioned amounts, leading near to bankruptcy absent foreign loans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation apportionment objection under the Articles
rubrics_metrics.description: The system of raising money by apportioning contributions according to the value of lands and improvements was criticized as unjust and impracticable because 'there can be no common measure of national wealth' and thus 'no general or stationary rule by which the ability of a state to pay taxes can be determined.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This perceived inequality and the reluctance of states to pay their quotas aggravated delays and evasion; from Nov. 1781 to Jan. 1786 Congress laid over $10,000,000 in requisitions but received less than one-fourth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial/commerce enforcement failures under the Articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Congress could regulate foreign commerce by treaty, in practice the Confederation was unable to enforce treaty stipulations on unwilling states; states imposed their own imposts and duties, bid against one another for trade, and engaged in interstate commercial conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The resulting disordered commerce included states discriminating against neighbors (e.g., Connecticut, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, New York) and laying duties that provoked inter-state strife; such dysfunctions were cited as reasons the confederation failed to protect commerce and property interests.
